Sie fährt. Sie schreit auf, sie weiß nicht, dass sie schreit, es schreit aus ihr, das Herz hat einen Mund und schreit. Der Wagen hält, sie springt aus ihm, leichtfüßig wie eine Junge. Menuchim sitzt noch auf der Schwelle. Sie fällt vor Menuchim nieder. „Mama, Mama!“, lallt Menuchim. Sie bleibt liegen.
units.en: Weeping, she gets into the carriage. She doesn't see the faces of the people whose hands she shakes. Her two eyes are two great seas full of tears. She hears the horses' hooves clattering. She is moving. She cries out; she doesn't know she is crying out; it cries out of her; the heart has a mouth and cries. The carriage stops, she jumps out of it, light-footed as a young girl. Menuchim is still sitting on the doorstep. She falls down in front of Menuchim. 'Mama, Mama!' babbles Menuchim. She stays lying there.
units.explain_en: Short sentences in the present tense show Deborah's despair. 'einsteigen' = to get in (a vehicle). 'die Hände drücken' = to shake hands. 'der Huf, die Hufe' = hoof. 'klappern' = to clatter. 'es schreit aus ihr' = 'it screams out of her' – the impersonal 'es' shows she has lost control. 'leichtfüßig' = light-footed. 'eine Junge' = a young woman. 'lallen' = to babble, to slur (like a baby or a drunk person).

units.de:
Die Familie Billes hebt Deborah hoch. Sie schreit, sie wehrt sich, sie bleibt schließlich still. Man trägt sie wieder zum Wagen und bettet sie auf das Heu. Der Wagen rollt sehr schnell nach Dubno.
Sechs Stunden später saßen sie in der Eisenbahn, im langsamen Personenzug, zusammen mit vielen unbekannten Menschen. Der Zug fuhr sachte durch das Land, die Wiesen und die Felder, auf denen man erntete, die Bauern und Bäuerinnen, die Hütten und Herden grüßten den Zug. Das sanfte Lied der Räder schläferte die Passagiere ein. Deborah hatte noch kein Wort gesprochen. Sie schlummerte. Die Räder der Eisenbahn wiederholten unaufhörlich, unaufhörlich: Verlass ihn nicht! Verlass ihn nicht! Verlass ihn nicht!
units.en:
The Billes family lifts Deborah up. She screams, she struggles, at last she goes quiet. They carry her back to the carriage and lay her in the hay. The carriage rolls very fast to Dubno.
Six hours later they were sitting on the train, the slow passenger train, together with many strangers. The train travelled gently through the countryside; the meadows and fields where people were harvesting, the peasant men and women, the huts and herds greeted the train. The gentle song of the wheels sent the passengers to sleep. Deborah hadn't said a word yet. She dozed. The wheels of the train repeated endlessly, endlessly: Don't leave him! Don't leave him! Don't leave him!
units.explain_en: Notice the change from present tense back to past tense: the terrible moment is over and the journey begins. 'sich wehren' = to struggle, to defend oneself. 'betten' = to lay (someone) down. 'der Personenzug' = slow passenger train (today 'der Regionalzug'). 'ernten' = to harvest. 'einschläfern' = to send to sleep. 'schlummern' = to doze, to slumber. The rhythm of the wheels repeats the rabbi's words: 'Verlass ihn nicht!'

units.en: On the train Kapturak's man flirts with Mirjam, and Mendel prays to calm his fear of the sea. They cross the border without problems and travel for three days, changing trains twice, to Bremen. There the families are counted, given tin number tags and put up for the night in a crowded barracks. The next morning they reach the big white ship 'Neptun'. The others are pushed below deck, but Mendel stays standing at the top of a narrow iron ladder, looking at the endless water. He thinks that God himself created the sea, and that deep down lives Leviathan, the holy fish, beside which even this huge ship is tiny.

units.de:
Nein, Mendel fühlte keine Angst. Er beruhigte den Matrosen, er, ein kleiner, schwarzer Jude auf einem riesengroßen Schiff und vor dem ewigen Ozean, er drehte sich noch einmal im Halbkreis und murmelte den Segen, der zu sprechen ist beim Anblick des Meeres. Er drehte sich im Halbkreis und verstreute die einzelnen Worte des Segens über die grünen Wogen: „Gelobt seist Du, Ewiger, unser Herr, der Du die Meere geschaffen hast und durch sie trennest die Kontinente!“
In diesem Augenblick erdröhnten die Sirenen. Die Maschinen begannen zu poltern. Und die Luft und das Schiff und die Menschen erzitterten. Nur der Himmel blieb still und blau, blau und still.
units.en:
No, Mendel felt no fear. He calmed the sailor – he, a small, black-clad Jew on an enormous ship and in front of the eternal ocean; he turned once more in a half-circle and murmured the blessing that is to be said at the sight of the sea. He turned in a half-circle and scattered the single words of the blessing over the green waves: 'Blessed are You, Eternal One, our Lord, who created the seas and through them separates the continents!'
At that moment the sirens roared. The engines began to rumble. And the air and the ship and the people shook. Only the sky stayed still and blue, blue and still.
units.explain_en: Mendel, who feared the journey, finds peace in his faith as the ship leaves Europe. 'der Matrose' = sailor. 'beruhigen' = to calm down. 'der Segen' = blessing – in Judaism there are blessings for many moments, even for seeing the sea. 'Gelobt seist Du' = Blessed/praised be You – 'seist' is Konjunktiv I of 'sein', used in prayers. 'trennen' = to separate; 'trennest' is an old poetic form of 'trennst'. 'erdröhnen' = to roar. 'erzittern' = to shake. Notice the mirror pattern at the end: 'still und blau, blau und still'.

units.en: On the fourteenth evening at sea, fireworks from lightships light up the sky, and a Jew who has made the journey before tells Mendel about the Statue of Liberty and its torch, which burns electrically. On the fifteenth day they land in New York. Men in uniforms without sabres check the passengers; Mendel thinks they must be the Cossacks of America. Nobody stabs their luggage with spears, and Deborah thinks sadly that they could have taken Menuchim with them after all.

units.de:
Auf einmal stand Schemarjah vor ihnen.
Alle drei erschraken auf die gleiche Weise.
Sie sahen gleichzeitig ihr altes Häuschen wieder, den alten Schemarjah und den neuen Schemarjah, genannt Sam.
Sie sahen Schemarjah und Sam zugleich, als wenn Sam über einen Schemarjah gestülpt worden wäre, ein durchsichtiger Sam.
Es war zwar Schemarjah, aber es war Sam.
Es waren zwei. Der eine trug eine schwarze Mütze, ein schwarzes Gewand und hohe Stiefel, und die ersten flaumigen, schwarzen Härchen sprossen aus den Poren seiner Wangen.
units.en:
All at once Schemarjah was standing in front of them.
All three of them got a fright in the same way.
At the same moment they saw their old house again, the old Schemarjah and the new Schemarjah, called Sam.
They saw Schemarjah and Sam at the same time, as if Sam had been pulled over a Schemarjah, a see-through Sam.
It was Schemarjah, true, but it was Sam.
There were two of them. One wore a black cap, a black gown and high boots, and the first downy black hairs were sprouting from the pores of his cheeks.
units.explain_en: A very clever passage: the parents see their son double – the boy who left home and the American he has become. 'erschrecken' = to get a fright. 'auf die gleiche Weise' = in the same way. 'gleichzeitig' / 'zugleich' = at the same time. 'genannt' = called, known as. 'über etwas stülpen' = to pull (something) over something. 'durchsichtig' = transparent, see-through. 'zwar ..., aber ...' = true ..., but ... 'flaumig' = downy, fluffy.

Der zweite trug einen hellgrauen Rock, eine schneeweiße Mütze wie der Kapitän, breite, gelbe Hosen, ein leuchtendes Hemd aus grüner Seide, und sein Angesicht war glatt wie ein nobler Grabstein.
Der zweite war beinahe Mac.
Der erste sprach mit seiner alten Stimme – sie hörten nur die Stimme, nicht die Worte.
Der zweite schlug mit einer starken Hand seinem Vater auf die Schulter und sagte, und jetzt erst hörten sie die Worte: „Hallo, old chap!“, und verstanden nichts.
Der erste war Schemarjah. Der zweite aber war Sam.
units.en:
The second wore a light grey jacket, a snow-white cap like the captain's, wide yellow trousers and a shiny green silk shirt, and his face was as smooth as a fine gravestone.
The second was almost Mac.
The first spoke with his old voice – they only heard the voice, not the words.
The second slapped his father on the shoulder with a strong hand and said – and only now did they hear the words – 'Hallo, old chap!', and they understood nothing.
The first was Schemarjah. But the second was Sam.
units.explain_en: The contrast between 'der erste' (the first) and 'der zweite' (the second) continues. 'hellgrau' = light grey; 'schneeweiß' = snow-white. 'die Seide' = silk. 'glatt' = smooth. 'der Grabstein' = gravestone – a strange, slightly frightening comparison. 'beinahe' = almost (today more often 'fast'). 'old chap' is English: Sam uses American phrases his father doesn't understand.

units.en: Sam kisses his parents and Mirjam; he smells of shaving soap, like a garden and a hospital at once. Despite Mac's promises, the family has to spend four days in quarantine before he manages to get them out. Then Mac insists that they see America from an open car of his firm. In the burning heat, the noise of trams and horns, the smells of tar, fish and petrol, Mendel keeps smiling and nodding helplessly while his son talks at him. America crushes him – and after a few minutes he faints. He wakes up in a lunch room, sees a stranger with a white beard in the mirror and only recognises himself from his family standing around him.

units.de: Was gehen mich diese Leute an? dachte Mendel. Was geht mich ganz Amerika an? Mein Sohn, meine Frau, meine Tochter, dieser Mac? Bin ich noch Mendel Singer? Ist das noch meine Familie? Bin ich noch Mendel Singer? Wo ist mein Sohn Menuchim? Es war ihm, als wäre er aus sich selbst herausgestoßen worden, von sich selbst getrennt, würde er fortan leben müssen. Es war ihm, als hätte er sich selbst in Zuchnow zurückgelassen, in der Nähe Menuchims. Und während es um seine Lippen lächelte und während es seinen Kopf schüttelte, begann sein Herz, langsam zu vereisen, es pochte wie ein metallener Schlegel gegen kaltes Glas. Schon war er einsam, Mendel Singer: Schon war er in Amerika…
units.en: What have these people to do with me? thought Mendel. What has the whole of America to do with me? My son, my wife, my daughter, this Mac? Am I still Mendel Singer? Is this still my family? Am I still Mendel Singer? Where is my son Menuchim? He felt as if he had been pushed out of himself, as if from now on he would have to live separated from himself. He felt as if he had left himself behind in Zuchnow, near Menuchim. And while something smiled around his lips and something shook his head, his heart slowly began to freeze; it knocked like a metal hammer against cold glass. Already he was lonely, Mendel Singer: already he was in America…
units.explain_en: The end of Part One: Mendel feels he has lost himself. 'Was geht mich das an?' = what has that got to do with me? – very common today. The repeated question 'Bin ich noch Mendel Singer?' shows his identity crisis. 'Es war ihm, als ...' = he felt as if ... (with Konjunktiv II: 'als wäre er ...'). 'fortan' = from now on (formal). 'es lächelte um seine Lippen' – impersonal 'es' again: the smile happens without him. 'vereisen' = to freeze over. 'einsam' = lonely.

sentences.en: And while something smiled around his lips and something shook his head, his heart slowly began to freeze; it knocked like a metal hammer against cold glass.

units.en: A few months later Mendel is almost at home in New York. He knows a few English words, lives with Deborah and Mirjam in a dark first-floor flat on the Lower East Side, surrounded by other Jews from Eastern Europe, and sleeps in the kitchen. Sam has a shop, a wife, Vega, and a baby son. Mirjam works as a sales assistant in Sam's shop and goes swimming and dancing with Mac, who isn't Jewish – but better Mac than the Cossacks, thinks Mendel. Deborah goes to the cinema and wears a silk dress, but she isn't happy: America seems just like a bigger version of the Jewish town at home, only darker, and money still doesn't last.

units.de:
Nein, sie wusste nicht genau, was ihr fehlte, Menuchim fehlte ihr. Oft, im Schlaf, im Wachen, beim Einkaufen, im Kino, beim Aufräumen, beim Backen hörte sie ihn rufen. Mama! Mama! rief er. Das einzige Wort, das er sprechen gelernt hatte, musste er jetzt schon vergessen haben. Fremde Kinder hörte sie Mama rufen, die Mütter meldeten sich, keine einzige Mutter ließ freiwillig von ihrem Kinde. Man hätte nicht nach Amerika fahren dürfen. Aber man konnte ja immer noch heimkehren!
„Mendel“, sagte sie manchmal, „sollen wir nicht umkehren, Menuchim sehen?“
units.en:
No, she didn't know exactly what she was missing – she was missing Menuchim. Often, asleep or awake, shopping, at the cinema, tidying up or baking, she heard him calling. Mama! Mama! he called. The only word he had learned to speak – he must have forgotten it by now. She heard other children calling Mama; the mothers answered; not a single mother would leave her child of her own free will. They should never have come to America. But they could still go home!
'Mendel', she sometimes said, 'shouldn't we go back and see Menuchim?'
units.explain_en: Deborah's guilt about Menuchim never leaves her. 'fehlen' = to be missing: 'Menuchim fehlte ihr' = she missed Menuchim (literally 'Menuchim was missing to her') – the person you miss is the subject! 'Du fehlst mir' = I miss you. 'beim Einkaufen, beim Aufräumen, beim Backen' = while shopping, tidying, baking ('beim' + verb as noun). 'sich melden' = to answer, to respond. 'freiwillig' = voluntarily. 'Man hätte nicht ... fahren dürfen' = they shouldn't have gone.

units.en: Mendel also thinks about going back, but Sam says it's too expensive right now: he and Mac are doing big business with building plots. Mendel spends his afternoons in the Skowronneks' music shop, where old men of the neighbourhood talk politics and pray. One evening Sam announces that he and Mac have made fifteen thousand dollars in one deal. The family celebrates with a trip to Atlantic City. When they come home, a fat letter is stuck in the door. 'This is a good letter,' says Mendel. 'Luck has begun.' It is from the Billes family in Zuchnow – and it says that Menuchim has suddenly begun to speak.

units.de: „Der Doktor Soltysiuk hat ihn gesehen“, schrieb die Familie Billes. „Er konnte es nicht glauben. Man will Menuchim nach Petersburg schicken, die großen Doktoren wollen sich den Kopf über ihn zerbrechen. Eines Tages, es war Donnerstagnachmittag, er war allein zu Haus, und es brannte im Ofen wie jeden Donnerstag, fiel ein brennendes Scheit heraus, und jetzt ist der ganze Fußboden verbrannt, und die Wände muss man tünchen. Es kostet ein schönes Stück Geld. Menuchim lief auf die Straße, er kann auch schon ganz gut laufen, und schrie: ‚Es brennt!‘ Und seit damals spricht er ein paar Worte.
units.en: 'Doctor Soltysiuk has seen him', wrote the Billes family. 'He couldn't believe it. They want to send Menuchim to Petersburg, the great doctors want to rack their brains over him. One day – it was a Thursday afternoon, he was alone at home, and the stove was burning like every Thursday – a burning log fell out, and now the whole floor is burnt and the walls need whitewashing. It costs a pretty penny. Menuchim ran out into the street – he can walk quite well already, too – and shouted: "Fire!" And since then he speaks a few words.'
units.explain_en: The miracle seems to be starting – through a fire. Doctor Soltysiuk is the doctor from the beginning of the book who wanted to treat Menuchim. 'sich den Kopf zerbrechen über' = to rack one's brains about – very common. 'das Scheit' = log (of wood). 'tünchen' = to whitewash, to paint. 'Es kostet ein schönes Stück Geld' = it costs a lot of money. 'Es brennt!' = Fire! (literally: it's burning) – what you shout in German in a fire. 'seit damals' = since then.

units.en: On the back of the letter there is a message from Jonas, who came to Zuchnow on leave and was amazed to learn that his family had gone to America. He writes that he is doing well: everyone is good to him, he loves the horses and can ride like the best Cossack. He wants to stay in the army, where one doesn't have to think for oneself. His captain has said he might ask the Tsar to pardon his deserter brother. But people are saying a war may come, he writes, and his parents must be prepared for him to die, as he himself is prepared.

units.de:
Mendel Singer legte die Brille ab, sah, dass Deborah weinte, und ergriff nach langen Jahren zum ersten Mal wieder ihre beiden Hände. Er zog ihre Hände vom verweinten Angesicht und sagte beinahe feierlich: „Nun, Deborah, der Herr hat uns geholfen. Nimm den Schal, geh hinunter, und bring eine Flasche Met.“
Sie saßen am Tisch und tranken den Met aus Teegläsern, sahen sich an und dachten das Gleiche. „Der Rabbi hat recht“, sagte Deborah. Deutlich diktierte ihr die Erinnerung die Worte, die lange in ihr geschlafen hatten: „Der Schmerz wird ihn weise machen, die Hässlichkeit gütig, die Bitternis milde und die Krankheit stark.“
units.en:
Mendel Singer took off his glasses, saw that Deborah was crying, and for the first time in many years took both her hands again. He pulled her hands away from her tear-stained face and said, almost solemnly: 'Well, Deborah, the Lord has helped us. Take your shawl, go downstairs and fetch a bottle of mead.'
They sat at the table and drank the mead out of tea glasses, looked at each other and thought the same thing. 'The rabbi was right', said Deborah. Memory clearly dictated to her the words that had long been asleep inside her: 'Pain will make him wise, ugliness kind, bitterness gentle and sickness strong.'
units.explain_en: A rare happy moment: Mendel and Deborah are close again, and Deborah remembers the prophecy from Chapter 1. 'die Brille ablegen' = to take off one's glasses (today usually 'abnehmen'). 'ergreifen' = to take, to grasp. 'verweint' = tear-stained. 'feierlich' = solemn(ly). 'der Met' = mead (a drink made of honey). 'das Gleiche denken' = to think the same thing. 'recht haben' = to be right – very important everyday phrase: 'Du hast recht!'

units.en: That night Mendel sings psalms until morning and even dances with joy. For the first time his worries leave him. Sam moves to a richer part of the city, but Mendel stays in his poor street among his friends: Menkes the fruit seller, Skowronnek, Rottenberg and Groschel. He is getting old and often falls asleep when his children visit, dreaming of the White House, of acrobats and of Menuchim. On hot summer nights full of bugs he stands at the window and longs for the starry sky of home. Mac offers to travel to Russia in summer to fetch Menuchim, and Mendel suspects he is doing it because he wants to marry Mirjam.

units.de:
Ende Juli bestellt Mac eine Schiffskarte. Man schreibt an die Familie Billes. Mendel geht in den Laden der Skowronneks, um den Freunden zu erzählen, dass sein jüngster Sohn ebenfalls nach Amerika kommt. Im Laden der Familie Skowronnek sind viel mehr Leute versammelt als sonst, an andern Tagen. Jeder hat ein Zeitungspapier in der Hand. In Europa ist der Krieg ausgebrochen.
Mac wird nicht mehr nach Russland fahren. Menuchim wird nicht nach Amerika kommen. Der Krieg ist ausgebrochen.
Hatten die Sorgen nicht soeben erst Mendel Singer verlassen? Sie gingen, und der Krieg brach aus.
Jonas war im Krieg und Menuchim in Russland.
units.en:
At the end of July Mac books a ship ticket. They write to the Billes family. Mendel goes to the Skowronneks' shop to tell his friends that his youngest son is coming to America too. In the Skowronneks' shop many more people have gathered than on other days. Everyone has a newspaper in his hand. In Europe war has broken out.
Mac won't go to Russia now. Menuchim won't come to America. War has broken out.
Hadn't his worries only just left Mendel Singer? They went, and the war broke out.
Jonas was in the war and Menuchim in Russia.
units.explain_en: The First World War (1914) destroys Mendel's new hopes. Roth uses the present tense for the news, then short, heavy sentences. 'eine Schiffskarte bestellen' = to book a ship ticket. 'versammelt sein' = to have gathered. 'die Zeitung' = newspaper. 'ausbrechen' = to break out (war, fire, disease): 'Der Krieg ist ausgebrochen.' 'soeben erst' = only just. 'die Sorgen' = worries.

units.en: The family tries to hide their fears from Mendel: Jonas is fighting for the Tsar, and Menuchim is somewhere in war-torn Russia. At night Mendel sings psalms, but feels it isn't enough. Then America enters the war too. Sam and Mac volunteer – as Mirjam explains, America is a real homeland, and it is a duty to fight for it. The Red Cross reports that Jonas is missing. Mirjam now goes out with Mr Glück, a manager in Sam's shop, and Mendel is angry when he sees how Glück behaves with both Mirjam and Sam's wife. One grey February day, while Mendel and Deborah are having lunch, Mirjam suddenly comes in during working hours and stands there without a word. Mendel feels he has dreamt this scene before and already knows what is coming.

units.de:
Es ist ein paar Sekunden still. Mirjam spricht nicht, als hoffte sie, der Vater oder die Mutter würden sie durch eine Frage von der Pflicht befreien, die Botschaft auszurichten. Sie steht und schweigt. Keins von den dreien rührt sich.
Mendel steht auf und sagt: „Ein Unglück ist geschehen!“
Mirjam sagt: „Mac ist zurückgekommen. Er hat Sams Uhr gebracht und die letzten Grüße.“
Deborah sitzt, als ob nichts geschehen wäre, ruhig auf dem Sessel. Ihre Augen sind trocken und leer wie zwei dunkle Stückchen Glas. Sie sitzt dem Fenster gegenüber, und es sieht aus, als zählte sie die Schneeflocken.
Es ist still, man hört das harte Ticken der Uhr.
units.en:
For a few seconds it is quiet. Mirjam doesn't speak, as if she were hoping that her father or mother would free her, by asking a question, from the duty of delivering the message. She stands and says nothing. None of the three moves.
Mendel stands up and says: 'Something terrible has happened!'
Mirjam says: 'Mac has come back. He has brought Sam's watch and his last greetings.'
Deborah sits quietly on the chair, as if nothing had happened. Her eyes are dry and empty like two dark little pieces of glass. She is sitting opposite the window, and it looks as if she were counting the snowflakes.
It is quiet; you can hear the hard ticking of the clock.
units.explain_en: Sam has been killed in the war. The present tense and very simple sentences make the news almost unbearable. 'als hoffte sie' = as if she were hoping (Konjunktiv II after 'als'). 'die Botschaft ausrichten' = to deliver a message ('Richte ihm Grüße aus!' = say hi to him from me). 'Ein Unglück ist geschehen' = something terrible has happened. 'die letzten Grüße' = last greetings (from a dying person). 'als ob nichts geschehen wäre' = as if nothing had happened. 'die Schneeflocke' = snowflake.

units.en: Suddenly Deborah slowly begins to tear out her hair, strand by strand, as calmly as the snow is falling outside. Mirjam sinks to her knees and hides her face in her mother's lap. Then Deborah begins to sing in a deep, strange voice – an old Jewish song without words, a lullaby for dead children. Mac comes in with Sam's watch, wallet and purse, puts them on the table in front of Deborah, lays his big hands on Mendel's shoulders and weeps silently. Night falls. Suddenly a groaning sound comes from Deborah's chest, like a broken note of her song.

Mac stößt die Tür auf, lässt sie offen, es wird kalt in der Stube.
Er kommt zurück, ein Doktor begleitet ihn, ein kleiner, flinker, grauhaariger Mann.
Mirjam steht dem Vater gegenüber.

units.en:
Then Deborah falls from the chair. She lies on the floor, a bent, soft mass.
Mac pushes the door open and leaves it open; it gets cold in the room.
He comes back, a doctor with him, a small, quick, grey-haired man.
Mirjam stands facing her father.
Mac and the doctor carry Deborah onto the bed.
The doctor sits on the edge of the bed and says: 'She is dead.'
Menuchim has died too, alone, among strangers, thinks Mendel Singer.

'der Bettrand' = edge of the bed. 'tot' = dead; 'sterben' (starb, ist gestorben) = to die. Mendel now believes that Menuchim must be dead too – he has lost all hope. 'unter Fremden' = among strangers.

units.en: For seven days Mendel sits on a low stool in mourning, as Jewish custom requires, with a white cloth on the window and a lamp burning day and night. Neighbours bring him round foods like eggs and bagels – round like mourning, without beginning or end. Mendel hardly notices them. Instead, he speaks silently to his dead wife:

units.de: „Du hast es gut, Deborah!“, sagte er zu ihr. „Es ist nur schade, dass du keinen Sohn hinterlassen hast, ich selbst muss das Totengebet sagen, ich werde aber bald sterben, und niemand wird uns beweinen. Wie zwei kleine Stäubchen wurden wir verweht. Wie zwei kleine Fünkchen sind wir erloschen. Ich habe Kinder gezeugt, dein Schoß hat sie geboren, der Tod hat sie genommen. Voller Not und ohne Sinn war dein Leben. In jungen Jahren habe ich dein Fleisch genossen, in späten Jahren habe ich es verschmäht. Vielleicht war das unsere Sünde.
units.en: 'You're well off, Deborah!' he said to her. 'It's just a pity you haven't left a son behind; I have to say the prayer for the dead myself, but I will die soon, and nobody will mourn us. We were blown away like two little specks of dust. We went out like two little sparks. I fathered children, your womb bore them, death has taken them. Your life was full of hardship and without meaning. In our young years I enjoyed your body, in later years I scorned it. Perhaps that was our sin.
units.explain_en: Mendel's lament for Deborah – Roth's language here sounds like the Bible. 'Du hast es gut' = you're lucky, you're well off – very common: 'Du hast es gut, du hast Ferien!' 'das Totengebet' = prayer for the dead (the Kaddish, traditionally said by a son). 'beweinen' = to mourn, to weep for. 'verwehen' = to blow away. 'erlöschen' (erlosch, ist erloschen) = to go out (fire, light). 'zeugen' = to father. 'verschmähen' = to scorn, to reject (formal). 'die Sünde' = sin.

Der Herr hat Mitleid mit dir gehabt. Du bist eine Tote und begraben. Mit mir hat Er kein Mitleid. Denn ich bin ein Toter und lebe. Er ist der Herr, Er weiß, was Er tut. Wenn du kannst, bete für mich, dass man mich auslösche aus dem Buch der Lebendigen.
units.en: Because there was no warmth of love in us, but between us the frost of habit, everything around us died, withered and was spoiled. You're well off, Deborah. The Lord has had pity on you. You are dead and buried. On me He has no pity. For I am a dead man and I live. He is the Lord, He knows what He is doing. If you can, pray for me that I may be blotted out of the Book of the Living.
units.explain_en: Mendel feels he is 'a dead man who is alive' and wishes to die. 'der Frost der Gewohnheit' = the frost of habit – a beautiful image of a cold marriage. 'verkümmern' = to wither, to waste away. 'Mitleid haben mit' = to have pity on – very common. 'begraben' = buried. 'Er weiß, was Er tut' = He knows what He is doing (capital 'Er' for God). 'auslöschen' = to blot out, to wipe out; 'auslösche' is Konjunktiv I after 'bete, dass man ...'. 'das Buch der Lebendigen' = the Book of Life (a Jewish image).

units.en: Mendel feels he is only 'the rest of Mendel Singer': America, he says, has killed them. On the eighth day he learns that Mirjam has had a breakdown. She laughs and sobs wildly, says shocking things about the men in her life, and has to be taken to a psychiatric hospital. The doctor says there is probably no cure and that Mendel should pray. Mendel tells Vega to marry Mac, not Mr Glück, and sends everyone away, feeling strangely free. Alone, he makes a fire in the kitchen stove and wants to burn his prayer shawl, prayer straps and prayer books, stamping and shouting, 'It's over, over, over with Mendel Singer!' But his hands refuse to throw them into the flames. The neighbours smell smoke and fetch his four old friends. They sit him on the bed, and Menkes asks why he wants to burn down the house.

Ihr werdet staunen und sagen: Auch Mendel ist verrückt, wie seine Tochter. Aber ich versichere euch: Ich bin nicht verrückt. Ich war verrückt. Mehr als sechzig Jahre war ich verrückt, heute bin ich es nicht.“
„Also sag uns, was du verbrennen willst!“
„Gott will ich verbrennen.“
units.en:
'I want to burn more than just a house and more than a human being. You will be amazed when I tell you what I really had in mind to burn. You will be amazed and say: Mendel has gone mad too, like his daughter. But I assure you: I am not mad. I was mad. For more than sixty years I was mad; today I am not.'
'So tell us what you want to burn!'
'God is what I want to burn.'
units.explain_en: Mendel, once the most devout man, turns against God – just like Job in the Bible. 'verbrennen' = to burn (something). 'staunen' = to be amazed. 'im Sinn haben' = to have in mind. 'verrückt' = mad, crazy – very common. 'versichern' = to assure (also: to insure). Notice the word order in the last sentence: 'Gott will ich verbrennen' puts 'Gott' first for shock – normal order would be 'Ich will Gott verbrennen.'

units.de: Allen vier Zuhörern entrang sich gleichzeitig ein Schrei. Sie waren nicht alle fromm und gottesfürchtig, wie Mendel immer gewesen war. Alle vier lebten schon lange genug in Amerika, sie arbeiteten am Sabbat, ihr Sinn stand nach Geld, und der Staub der Welt lag schon dicht, hoch und grau auf ihrem alten Glauben. Viele Bräuche hatten sie vergessen, gegen manche Gesetze hatten sie verstoßen, mit ihren Köpfen und Gliedern hatten sie gesündigt. Aber Gott wohnte noch in ihren Herzen. Und als Mendel Gott lästerte, war es ihnen, als hätte er mit scharfen Fingern an ihre nackten Herzen gegriffen.
units.en: All four listeners cried out at the same time. They were not all as pious and God-fearing as Mendel had always been. All four had lived in America long enough; they worked on the Sabbath, their minds were set on money, and the dust of the world already lay thick, high and grey on their old faith. They had forgotten many customs, broken many laws, sinned with their heads and their limbs. But God still lived in their hearts. And when Mendel blasphemed against God, they felt as if he had reached into their naked hearts with sharp fingers.
units.explain_en: The friends are not perfect believers, but Mendel's words still shock them deeply. 'fromm' = pious, devout. 'gottesfürchtig' = God-fearing. 'der Sabbat' = the Sabbath (Jewish day of rest, Friday evening to Saturday evening), when religious Jews don't work. 'der Sinn stand ihnen nach Geld' = they were keen on money. 'der Brauch, die Bräuche' = custom. 'gegen ein Gesetz verstoßen' = to break a law. 'lästern' = to blaspheme; also colloquial 'to gossip about someone' ('über jemanden lästern').

„Lästere nicht, Mendel“, sagte nach einem längeren Schweigen Skowronnek. „Du weißt besser als ich, denn du hast viel mehr gelernt, dass Gottes Schläge einen verborgenen Sinn haben. Wir wissen nicht, wofür wir gestraft werden.“
„Ich aber weiß es, Skowronnek“, erwiderte Mendel. „Gott ist grausam, und je mehr man ihm gehorcht, desto strenger geht er mit uns um. Er ist mächtiger als die Mächtigen, mit dem Nagel seines kleinen Fingers kann er ihnen den Garaus machen, aber er tut es nicht. Nur die Schwachen vernichtet er gerne.
units.en:
'Don't blaspheme, Mendel', said Skowronnek after a long silence. 'You know better than I do, because you have studied much more, that God's blows have a hidden meaning. We don't know what we are being punished for.'
'But I know, Skowronnek', replied Mendel. 'God is cruel, and the more you obey him, the harder he is on us. He is mightier than the mighty; with the nail of his little finger he could finish them off, but he doesn't do it. It's only the weak he likes to destroy.
units.explain_en: The friends try the classic answer to suffering: God has a hidden purpose. Mendel disagrees bitterly. 'der Schlag, die Schläge' = blow, stroke. 'verborgen' = hidden. 'strafen' = to punish. 'grausam' = cruel. 'je mehr ..., desto ...' = the more ..., the more ... – very useful: 'Je mehr ich lerne, desto mehr weiß ich.' 'gehorchen' (+ dative) = to obey. 'jemandem den Garaus machen' = to finish someone off (old-fashioned idiom). 'vernichten' = to destroy.

units.de: Die Schwäche eines Menschen reizt seine Stärke, und der Gehorsam weckt seinen Zorn. Er ist ein großer, grausamer Isprawnik. Befolgst du die Gesetze, so sagt er, du habest sie nur zu deinem Vorteil befolgt. Und verstößt du nur gegen ein einziges Gebot, so verfolgt er dich mit hundert Strafen. Willst du ihn bestechen, so macht er dir einen Prozess. Und gehst du redlich mit ihm um, so lauert er auf die Bestechung. In ganz Russland gibt es keinen böseren Isprawnik!“
units.en: A person's weakness provokes his strength, and obedience arouses his anger. He is a big, cruel Isprawnik. If you obey the laws, he says you only obeyed them for your own advantage. And if you break just one single commandment, he pursues you with a hundred punishments. If you try to bribe him, he takes you to court. And if you deal honestly with him, he lies in wait for the bribe. In the whole of Russia there is no more wicked Isprawnik!'
units.explain_en: Mendel compares God to an 'Isprawnik' – a corrupt Russian district police chief of the Tsar's time, whom poor Jews feared. The sentences 'Befolgst du ..., so ...' are conditional sentences starting with the verb (= 'Wenn du ... befolgst, dann ...') – still used in written German. 'reizen' = to provoke. 'der Vorteil' = advantage. 'das Gebot' = commandment (die Zehn Gebote = the Ten Commandments). 'bestechen' = to bribe; 'die Bestechung' = bribery. 'redlich' = honest(ly). 'lauern auf' = to lie in wait for.

units.de: „Erinnere dich, Mendel“, begann Rottenberg, „erinnere dich an Hiob. Ihm ist Ähnliches geschehen wie dir. Er saß auf der nackten Erde, Asche auf dem Haupt, und seine Wunden taten ihm so weh, dass er sich wie ein Tier auf dem Boden wälzte. Auch er lästerte Gott. Und doch war es nur eine Prüfung gewesen. Was wissen wir, Mendel, was oben vorgeht? Vielleicht kam der Böse vor Gott und sagte wie damals: Man muss einen Gerechten verführen. Und der Herr sagte: Versuch es nur mit Mendel, meinem Knecht.“
units.en: 'Remember, Mendel', began Rottenberg, 'remember Job. Something similar happened to him as to you. He sat on the bare earth, ashes on his head, and his wounds hurt him so much that he rolled on the ground like an animal. He too blasphemed against God. And yet it had only been a test. What do we know, Mendel, of what goes on up there? Perhaps the Evil One came before God and said, like that time: One must lead a righteous man astray. And the Lord said: Just try it with Mendel, my servant.'
units.explain_en: Here the novel names its model: the Book of Job (German: 'Hiob') in the Bible, in which God allows Satan to test a righteous man with terrible suffering. 'sich erinnern an' = to remember. 'Ähnliches' = something similar (adjective used as a noun, so capitalised). 'die Asche' = ashes (a sign of mourning). 'die Wunde' = wound. 'sich wälzen' = to roll about. 'die Prüfung' = test, exam – also used for school exams! 'der Böse' = the Evil One (the devil). 'der Gerechte' = righteous man. 'der Knecht' = servant (old).

units.en: The friends keep arguing with Mendel: perhaps God still works smaller miracles; Menuchim and Jonas may be alive, Mirjam may get well. Mendel refuses to be comforted. The friends stay with him all night and then take him to the Skowronneks' shop, where he lives from now on in a windowless back room. Mendel stops praying and does odd jobs for the neighbours. On Yom Kippur, the holiest day, he stands silent at the back while the others pray. Vega marries Mac, as Mendel advised; Mirjam doesn't get better. When the war finally ends, everyone goes out to celebrate and Mendel is alone in the shop. For the first time he plays a new record from Europe – a beautiful song that makes him cry for the first time in years.

units.de:
So traf ihn der heimkehrende Skowronnek. Er stellte das Grammophon ab und sagte: „Mendel, zünde die Lampe an! Was spielst du hier?“ Mendel zündete die Lampe an. „Sieh nach, Skowronnek, wie das Liedchen heißt.“ „Das sind die neuen Platten“, sagte Skowronnek. „Heute habe ich sie gekauft. Das Lied heißt“ – Skowronnek zog die Brille an, hielt die Platte unter die Lampe und las: „Das Lied heißt «Menuchims Lied».“
Mendel wurde plötzlich schwach. Er musste sich setzen. Er starrte auf die spiegelnde Platte in Skowronneks Händen.
„Ich weiß, woran du denkst“, sagte Skowronnek.
„Ja“, antwortete Mendel.
units.en:
That's how Skowronnek found him when he came home. He switched off the gramophone and said: 'Mendel, light the lamp! What are you playing here?' Mendel lit the lamp. 'Look and see, Skowronnek, what the little song is called.' 'Those are the new records', said Skowronnek. 'I bought them today. The song is called' – Skowronnek put on his glasses, held the record under the lamp and read: 'The song is called "Menuchim's Song".'
Mendel suddenly felt weak. He had to sit down. He stared at the shining record in Skowronnek's hands.
'I know what you're thinking of', said Skowronnek.
'Yes', answered Mendel.
units.explain_en: A mysterious coincidence – or the beginning of a miracle? 'das Grammophon' = gramophone, an old record player. 'die Platte' = record (today also 'die Schallplatte'). 'abstellen' = to switch off (today often 'ausmachen'). 'anzünden' = to light. 'Wie heißt das Lied?' = what's the song called? – 'heißen' is used for names of things too. 'sich setzen' = to sit down. 'woran denkst du?' = what are you thinking of? ('denken an' + accusative).

Skowronnek drehte noch einmal die Kurbel. „Ein schönes Lied“, sagte Skowronnek, legte den Kopf auf die linke Schulter und horchte. Allmählich füllte sich der Laden mit den verspäteten Nachbarn. Keiner sprach. Alle hörten das Lied und wiegten im Takt die Köpfe.
Und sie hörten es sechzehn Mal, bis sie es auswendig konnten.
Mendel blieb allein im Laden. Er versperrte sorgfältig die Tür von innen, räumte das Schaufenster aus, begann sich auszuziehen. Jeden seiner Schritte begleitete das Lied. Während er einschlief, schien es ihm, dass sich die blaue und silberne Melodie mit dem kläglichen Wimmern verbinde, mit Menuchims, seines eigenen Menuchims, einzigem, längst nicht mehr gehörtem Lied.
units.en:
Skowronnek turned the crank once more. 'A beautiful song', said Skowronnek, tilted his head onto his left shoulder and listened. Gradually the shop filled with neighbours coming home late. Nobody spoke. Everyone listened to the song and rocked their heads to the beat.
And they listened to it sixteen times, until they knew it by heart.
Mendel stayed alone in the shop. He carefully locked the door from inside, cleared the shop window and began to undress. The song accompanied every step he took. As he fell asleep, it seemed to him that the blue and silver melody joined with the pitiful whimpering – with Menuchim's, his own Menuchim's, only song, not heard for so long.
units.explain_en: The song brings the neighbours together and brings back memories of Menuchim's whimpering. 'die Kurbel drehen' = to turn the crank (old gramophones were wound up by hand). 'horchen' = to listen carefully. 'allmählich' = gradually – very useful. 'im Takt' = in time (to the beat). 'auswendig können' = to know by heart – very common: 'Ich kann das Gedicht auswendig.' 'versperren' = to lock (today in Germany mostly 'abschließen'; 'zusperren' in Austria). 'das Wimmern' = whimpering.

units.en: In spring Mendel seems strangely happy. Secretly he takes Deborah's hidden savings from under a floorboard in their old flat: he wants to go home to Zuchnow to die there. The ice-cream seller Frisch tells him about a wonderful concert of an orchestra from Europe that played 'Menuchim's Song'. Its young conductor, Alexej Kossak – a relative of Deborah's – is looking for Mendel. Frisch shows him Kossak's photo, and Mendel cannot stop looking at the bright, wise eyes, like the eyes of a prophet. On the first evening of Passover Mendel sits at the end of the Skowronneks' table. As tradition requires, Mendel opens the door for the prophet Elijah. A minute later there is a knock. Everyone freezes – could it really be the prophet? Mendel opens the door: a tall stranger asks politely if he may come in.

units.de:
Es ist ein feiner Mann, dachte Skowronnek. Und er knöpfte, ohne ein Wort zu sagen, dem Fremden den Mantel auf. Der Mann verneigte sich und sagte: „Ich heiße Alexej Kossak. Ich bitte um Entschuldigung. Ich bitte sehr um Entschuldigung. Man hat mir gesagt, dass sich ein gewisser Mendel Singer aus Zuchnow bei Ihnen aufhält. Ich möchte ihn sprechen.“
„Das bin ich“, sagte Mendel, trat nahe an den Gast und hob den Kopf. Seine Stirn reichte bis zur Schulter des Fremden. „Herr Kossak“, fuhr Mendel fort, „ich habe schon von Ihnen gehört. Ein Verwandter sind Sie.“
„Legen Sie ab, und setzen Sie sich mit uns an den Tisch“, sagte Skowronnek.
units.en:
He's a fine gentleman, thought Skowronnek. And without saying a word he unbuttoned the stranger's coat. The man bowed and said: 'My name is Alexej Kossak. Please forgive me. I really do beg your pardon. I was told that a certain Mendel Singer from Zuchnow is staying with you. I would like to speak to him.'
'That's me', said Mendel, went up close to the guest and raised his head. His forehead came up to the stranger's shoulder. 'Mr Kossak', Mendel went on, 'I have already heard about you. You are a relative.'

units.en: Kossak sits opposite Mendel and politely waits until the Passover songs and the meal are finished. The two keep looking at each other; only the stranger's eyes seem familiar to Mendel. Then Kossak explains: after the war nobody knew where Mendel lived. He has bought Mendel's old house in Zuchnow and brought him the money: three hundred dollars. Jonas has been missing since 1915, but someone heard that he is alive and fighting in the White Army in Russia. Asked about his life, Kossak says he was a sick child and the son of a poor teacher, was cured in a hospital in a big city, discovered music and became a conductor. Mendel wants to ask about Menuchim, but he is too afraid of hearing that he is dead. So his friend Skowronnek asks for him:

„Mein Freund Mendel hatte noch einen armen, kranken Sohn namens Menuchim. Was ist mit ihm geschehen?“
Wieder antwortete der Fremde nicht. Er stocherte mit dem Löffel auf dem Grunde des Glases herum, zerrieb den Zucker, und als wollte er aus dem Tee die Antwort ablesen, sah er auf das hellbraune Glas, und den Löffel immer noch zwischen Daumen und Zeigefinger, die schmale, braune Hand sachte bewegend, sagte er endlich, unerwartet laut, wie mit einem plötzlichen Entschluss:
„Menuchim lebt!“
units.en:
'My friend Mendel had another son, a poor, sick boy called Menuchim. What has happened to him?'
Again the stranger didn't answer. He poked about with his spoon at the bottom of his glass, crushed the sugar, and as if he wanted to read the answer in the tea, he looked at the light brown glass; and still holding the spoon between thumb and forefinger, gently moving his slim brown hand, he said at last, unexpectedly loudly, as if he had made a sudden decision:
'Menuchim is alive!'

units.de: Es klingt nicht wie eine Antwort, es klingt wie ein Ruf. Unmittelbar darauf bricht ein Lachen aus Mendel Singers Brust. Alle erschrecken und sehen starr auf den Alten. Mendel sitzt zurückgelehnt auf dem Sessel, schüttelt sich und lacht. Sein Rücken ist so gebeugt, dass er die Lehne nicht ganz berühren kann. Zwischen der Lehne und Mendels altem Nacken (weiße Härchen kräuseln sich über dem schäbigen Kragen des Rocks) ist ein weiter Abstand. Mendels langer Bart bewegt sich heftig, flattert beinahe wie eine weiße Fahne und scheint ebenfalls zu lachen. Aus Mendels Brust dröhnt und kichert es abwechselnd.
units.en: It doesn't sound like an answer, it sounds like a call. Immediately afterwards a laugh bursts from Mendel Singer's chest. Everyone gets a fright and stares at the old man. Mendel sits leaning back in the armchair, shaking and laughing. His back is so bent that he can't quite touch the back of the chair. Between the back of the chair and Mendel's old neck (little white hairs curl above the shabby collar of his coat) there is a wide gap. Mendel's long beard moves wildly, flutters almost like a white flag and seems to be laughing too. From Mendel's chest comes booming and giggling by turns.

Alle erschrecken, Skowronnek erhebt sich etwas schwerfällig aus den schwellenden Kissen und behindert durch den langen, weißen Kittel, geht um den ganzen Tisch, tritt zu Mendel, beugt sich zu ihm und nimmt mit beiden Händen Mendels beide Hände. Da verwandelt sich Mendels Lachen in Weinen, er schluchzt, und die Tränen fließen aus den alten, halb verhüllten Augen in den wild wuchernden Bart, verlieren sich im wüsten Gestrüpp, andere bleiben lange und rund und voll wie gläserne Tropfen in den Haaren hängen.
Endlich ist Mendel ruhig. Er sieht Kossak gerade an und wiederholt: „Menuchim lebt?“
Der Fremde sieht Mendel ruhig an und sagt: „Menuchim lebt, er ist gesund, es geht ihm sogar gut!“
units.en:
Everyone is frightened. Skowronnek rises rather heavily from the swelling cushions and, hampered by the long white robe, walks round the whole table, steps up to Mendel, bends over him and takes both of Mendel's hands in both of his. Then Mendel's laughter turns into weeping; he sobs, and the tears flow from his old, half-hidden eyes into his wildly growing beard, lose themselves in the tangled undergrowth; others stay hanging in the hairs for a long time, round and full like glass drops.
At last Mendel is calm. He looks straight at Kossak and repeats: 'Menuchim is alive?'
The stranger looks calmly at Mendel and says: 'Menuchim is alive, he is well, he is even doing well!'
units.explain_en: At the Passover meal the head of the house traditionally sits on cushions and wears a white robe (der Kittel). 'schwerfällig' = heavily, clumsily. 'behindert durch' = hampered by. 'sich verwandeln in' = to turn into. 'schluchzen' = to sob. 'das Gestrüpp' = undergrowth, brushwood – a funny image for a wild beard. 'der Tropfen' = drop. 'gerade ansehen' = to look straight at. 'Es geht ihm gut' = he is doing well – one of the most important everyday phrases.

Mendel faltet die Hände, er hebt sie, so hoch er kann, dem Plafond entgegen. Er möchte aufstehen. Er hat das Gefühl, dass er jetzt aufstehen müsste, gerade werden, wachsen, groß und größer werden, über das Haus hinauf und mit den Händen den Himmel berühren. Er kann die gefalteten Hände nicht mehr lösen. Er blickt zu Skowronnek, und der alte Freund weiß, was er jetzt zu fragen hat, an Mendels Statt.
„Wo ist Menuchim jetzt?“, fragt Skowronnek.
Und langsam erwidert Alexej Kossak:
„Ich selbst bin Menuchim.“
units.en:
Mendel folds his hands and raises them as high as he can, towards the ceiling. He would like to stand up. He has the feeling that he ought to stand up now, become straight, grow, become big and bigger, up over the house, and touch the sky with his hands. He can no longer unclasp his folded hands. He looks at Skowronnek, and his old friend knows what he now has to ask in Mendel's place.
'Where is Menuchim now?' asks Skowronnek.
And slowly Alexej Kossak replies:
'I myself am Menuchim.'

'der Plafond' = ceiling – Austrian/old; in Germany today 'die Decke'. 'das Gefühl haben' = to have the feeling. 'berühren' = to touch. 'lösen' = to loosen, to release; also 'to solve' (a problem). 'an jemandes Statt' = in someone's place (old; today 'an seiner Stelle' or 'statt seiner'). 'erwidern' = to reply.

units.en: Everyone jumps up, the children wake and cry. Mendel falls on his knees before his son, kisses his hands and touches his face like a blind man, until Menuchim says 'Stand up, Father!' and lifts him onto his lap like a child. Mendel remembers the rabbi's words. Skowronnek fetches the other friends to see the miracle, and Mendel says God has overlooked his great sins. He takes his dusty bag with the prayer things from the nail, gives three hundred dollars to the poor and drives with his son to a grand hotel on Broadway. That night Menuchim tells his earliest memories: his father ringing a spoon against a glass, a fire, a hospital, a piano. He promises to find doctors for Mirjam. In the morning they drive out of the city, and Mendel doesn't want to know where: 'Wherever you drive, it's good.'

units.de: Und sie gelangten in eine Welt, wo der weiche Sand gelb war, das weite Meer blau und alle Häuser weiß. Auf der Terrasse vor einem dieser Häuser, an einem kleinen, weißen Tischchen, saß Mendel Singer. Er schlürfte einen goldbraunen Tee. Auf seinen gebeugten Rücken schien die erste warme Sonne dieses Jahres. Die Amseln hüpften dicht an ihn heran. Ihre Schwestern flöteten indessen vor der Terrasse. Die Wellen des Meeres plätscherten mit sanftem, regelmäßigem Schlag an den Strand. Am blassblauen Himmel standen ein paar weiße Wölkchen.
units.en: And they came into a world where the soft sand was yellow, the wide sea blue and all the houses white. On the terrace in front of one of these houses, at a small white table, sat Mendel Singer. He was sipping a golden-brown tea. The first warm sun of the year was shining on his bent back. The blackbirds hopped close up to him. Their sisters were meanwhile whistling in front of the terrace. The waves of the sea lapped against the shore with a soft, regular beat. A few little white clouds stood in the pale blue sky.
units.explain_en: The last part of the novel is full of light, colour and peace – the opposite of the dark flat in New York. 'gelangen' = to reach, to arrive (formal; today 'ankommen'). 'schlürfen' = to sip, to slurp. 'die Amsel' = blackbird (a very common bird in Germany). 'hüpfen' = to hop. 'flöten' = to whistle like a flute. 'plätschern' = to lap, to splash gently. 'regelmäßig' = regular. 'blassblau' = pale blue; 'das Wölkchen' = little cloud ('-chen' makes things small and neuter).

units.de: Unter diesem Himmel war es Mendel recht, zu glauben, dass Jonas sich einmal wieder einfinden würde und Mirjam heimkehren, „schöner als alle Frauen der Welt“, zitierte er im Stillen. Er selbst, Mendel Singer, wird nach späten Jahren in den guten Tod eingehen, umringt von vielen Enkeln und „satt am Leben“, wie es im „Hiob“ geschrieben stand. Er fühlte ein merkwürdiges und auch verbotenes Verlangen, die Mütze aus altem Seidenrips abzulegen und die Sonne auf seinen alten Schädel scheinen zu lassen. Und zum ersten Mal in seinem Leben entblößte Mendel Singer aus freiem Willen sein Haupt, so wie er es nur im Amt getan hatte und im Bad.
units.en: Under this sky Mendel was glad to believe that Jonas would turn up again one day and Mirjam would come home, 'fairer than all the women in the world', he quoted to himself. He himself, Mendel Singer, would, after many more years, pass into a good death, surrounded by many grandchildren and 'full of days', as it was written in 'Job'. He felt a strange and also forbidden longing to take off his old silk cap and let the sun shine on his old skull. And for the first time in his life Mendel Singer bared his head of his own free will, as he had only ever done before officials and in the bath.
units.explain_en: Mendel finds hope again. 'Es war ihm recht' = he was happy to, it suited him. 'sich einfinden' = to turn up (formal). 'zitieren' = to quote. 'satt am Leben' ('full of days, satisfied with life') is how the Bible describes Job's peaceful death. Religious Jewish men keep their heads covered as a sign of respect for God, so taking off his cap is a small, brave act of freedom. 'das Verlangen' = longing, desire. 'der Schädel' = skull. 'entblößen' = to bare, to uncover. 'aus freiem Willen' = of his own free will.

Die spärlichen, gekräuselten Härchen auf seinem kahlen Kopf bewegte ein Frühlingswind wie seltsame, zarte Pflanzen.
So grüßte Mendel Singer die Welt.
Und eine Möwe stieß wie ein silbernes Geschoss des Himmels unter das Zeltdach der Terrasse. Mendel beobachtete ihren jähen Flug und die schattenhafte, weiße Spur, die sie in der blauen Luft hinterließ.
Da sagte der Sohn: „Nächste Woche fahre ich nach San Francisco. Auf der Rückkehr spielen wir noch zehn Tage in Chicago. Ich denke, Vater, dass wir in vier Wochen nach Europa fahren können!“
units.en:
A spring wind moved the thin, curly little hairs on his bald head like strange, delicate plants.
That was how Mendel Singer greeted the world.
And a seagull shot like a silver arrow of the sky under the awning of the terrace. Mendel watched its sudden flight and the shadowy white trail it left behind in the blue air.
Then his son said: 'Next week I'm going to San Francisco. On the way back we'll play another ten days in Chicago. I think, Father, that in four weeks we can go to Europe!'
units.explain_en: 'So grüßte Mendel Singer die Welt' – a short sentence standing alone to mark a new beginning. 'spärlich' = sparse, thin. 'gekräuselt' = curly. 'kahl' = bald. 'zart' = delicate, tender. 'die Möwe' = seagull. 'das Geschoss' = projectile, bullet (here like an arrow). 'das Zeltdach' = awning (literally: tent roof). 'jäh' = sudden (literary; today 'plötzlich'). 'die Spur' = trail, track. Notice that Menuchim now calls Mendel 'Vater' – they are going to Europe together.

They drive back to the hotel. Menuchim tells his tired father to lie down on the sofa for a nap and goes out. Mendel lies down obediently. He knows where his son is going: to see his sister. A blessing rests on this wonderful man, he thinks – he will make Mirjam well.

Mendel erblickte eine große Fotografie in rostbraunem Rahmen auf dem kleinen Spiegeltisch. „Gib mir das Bild!“, bat er.
Er betrachtete es lange. Er sah die junge, blonde Frau in einem hellen Kleid, hell wie der Tag, in einem Garten saß sie, durch den der Wind spazieren ging und die Sträucher am Rande der Beete bewegte. Zwei Kinder, ein Mädchen und ein Knabe, standen neben einem kleinen, eselbespannten Wagen, wie sie in manchen Gärten als spielerisches Vehikel gebraucht werden.
„Gott segne sie!“, sagte Mendel.
units.en:
Mendel caught sight of a large photograph in a rust-brown frame on the little dressing table. 'Give me the picture!' he asked.
He looked at it for a long time. He saw the young blonde woman in a light dress, bright as day; she was sitting in a garden through which the wind was taking a walk, moving the bushes at the edges of the flowerbeds. Two children, a girl and a boy, were standing next to a small donkey cart, of the kind used in some gardens as a toy vehicle.
'God bless them!' said Mendel.
units.explain_en: Mendel discovers that Menuchim has a family of his own. 'erblicken' = to catch sight of (formal; today 'sehen'). 'der Rahmen' = frame. 'rostbraun' = rust-brown. 'betrachten' = to look at carefully. 'spazieren gehen' = to go for a walk – here the wind 'goes for a walk' through the garden (personification). 'der Strauch, die Sträucher' = bush. 'das Beet' = flowerbed. 'eselbespannt' = pulled by a donkey. 'Gott segne sie!' = God bless them! – 'segne' is Konjunktiv I for a wish.

units.de: Der Sohn ging. Der Vater blieb auf dem Sofa, die Fotografie legte er sachte neben sich. Sein müdes Auge schweifte durchs Zimmer zum Fenster. Von seinem tiefgelagerten Sofa aus konnte er einen vielgezackten, wolkenlosen Ausschnitt des Himmels sehen. Er nahm noch einmal das Bild vor. Da war seine Schwiegertochter, Menuchims Frau, da waren die Enkel, Menuchims Kinder. Betrachtete er das Mädchen genauer, glaubte er, ein Kinderbild Deborahs zu sehen. Tot war Deborah, mit fremden, jenseitigen Augen erlebte sie vielleicht das Wunder.
units.en: The son left. The father stayed on the sofa; he laid the photograph gently beside him. His tired eye wandered through the room to the window. From his low sofa he could see a jagged, cloudless patch of sky. He picked up the picture once more. There was his daughter-in-law, Menuchim's wife; there were the grandchildren, Menuchim's children. When he looked more closely at the girl, he thought he saw a childhood picture of Deborah. Deborah was dead; with strange eyes from the other world she was perhaps witnessing the miracle.
units.explain_en: Mendel thinks of Deborah, who did not live to see the miracle she hoped for all her life. 'schweifen' = to wander (eyes, thoughts). 'der Ausschnitt' = section, patch. 'die Schwiegertochter' = daughter-in-law ('Schwieger-' = in-law: der Schwiegersohn, die Schwiegermutter). 'der Enkel' = grandchild. 'genauer betrachten' = to look more closely. 'das Kinderbild' = childhood photo. 'jenseitig' = from the other world, beyond ('das Jenseits' = the afterlife). 'erleben' = to experience, to witness.

units.de: Dankbar erinnerte sich Mendel an ihre junge Wärme, die er einst gekostet hatte, ihre roten Wangen, ihre halboffenen Augen, die im Dunkel der Liebesnächte geleuchtet hatten, schmale, lockende Lichter. Tote Deborah! Er stand auf, schob einen Sessel an das Sofa, stellte das Bild auf den Sessel und legte sich wieder hin. Während sie sich langsam schlossen, nahmen seine Augen die ganze blaue Heiterkeit des Himmels in den Schlaf hinüber und die Gesichter der neuen Kinder. Neben ihnen tauchten aus dem braunen Hintergrund des Porträts Jonas und Mirjam auf. Mendel schlief ein. Und er ruhte aus von der Schwere des Glücks und der Größe der Wunder.
units.en: Gratefully Mendel remembered her young warmth, which he had once tasted, her red cheeks, her half-open eyes that had shone in the dark of their nights of love, narrow, alluring lights. Dead Deborah! He got up, pushed an armchair up to the sofa, stood the picture on the armchair and lay down again. As they slowly closed, his eyes took all the blue brightness of the sky with them into sleep, and the faces of the new children. Beside them, out of the brown background of the portrait, Jonas and Mirjam appeared. Mendel fell asleep. And he rested from the weight of happiness and the greatness of the miracles.
units.explain_en: The last lines of the novel. Mendel remembers the love of his young years with Deborah and falls asleep in peace – with all his children, the living and the lost, together in his mind. 'dankbar' = grateful(ly). 'sich erinnern an' = to remember. 'kosten' = to taste (also: to cost). 'lockend' = alluring, tempting. 'die Heiterkeit' = brightness, cheerfulness. 'auftauchen' = to appear, to surface. 'sich ausruhen von' = to rest from. The final sentence reverses the usual idea: not the weight of suffering, but 'die Schwere des Glücks' (the weight of happiness).
